source.title: Distilling Double Descent
source.authors: Andrew Cotter; A. Menon; Harikrishna Narasimhan; A. S. Rawat; Sashank J. Reddi; Yichen Zhou

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps model complexity and measures test error, directly testing model-wise double descent in its toy, CNN, ResNet, and random-feature settings. The architectures and datasets differ from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The reported test-error-versus-complexity curves are recorded below. Table 1's data counts are setup details, not results of a sample-size sweep. Figure 6 measures test entropy over training batches, not test error over epochs, so it does not test V2. The theoretical discussion of estimation error decreasing with unlabeled sample size is not an experimental test of V3. Entropy and cross-entropy results are not rows for the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper's purpose is distillation, and it says it takes double descent as given. But its teacher curves are Nakkiran-style width sweeps (filter multiplier m from 1 to 64, test error) on CIFAR-10, SVHN and ImageNet. It states where a clear double-descent pattern appears and where it does not. That is direct evidence on V1. The Belkin-style random-ReLU toy bears on V4. The CIFAR-10 label-noise sweep bears on V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors conclude that an overparameterized teacher can label a large unlabeled set, so that a simple student overfits less and outperforms an equally simple model trained directly; on CIFAR-10 only the soft student does so, and only at very low complexity. Soft labels beat hard labels, but hard labels work well too. The authors add that the 'dark knowledge' explanation is therefore incomplete. They explicitly do not test or explain double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses model-complexity sweeps and test error as in double-descent experiments, but applies them to distillation with its own toy, CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet settings and model configurations.
record.method_sensitivity: The presence and strength of the curve vary by dataset/model setting; student curves are weaker than teacher curves. Injected label noise on CIFAR-10 shifts the hump right. Soft versus hard labels changes student performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Teacher test cross-entropy decreases with complexity beyond a point, though it never beats the best classical model (Figure 7). Teacher test entropy does not converge to a hard classifier (Figures 4 and 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In overparameterized networks, test cross-entropy also shows a second descent, while test-set predictions stay soft.

record.problems: The main experiments use single runs because of resource costs. The paper provides five-run ranges only for CIFAR-10 student runs from the m = 64 teacher. Many relevant curve values are presented only in figures, without exact numeric values.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant test-error-versus-complexity results were left out. Figure 6's test-entropy-over-training-batches curves and Figure 4/8 entropy curves were not cataloged as rows because they do not measure the test error named by the versions tested here.

untested.parts: Only width (filter-multiplier) sweeps with Adam at constant learning rate, single runs. The peak location relative to the interpolation threshold is not quantified beyond stated memorization points.
Not tested. Figure 6 plots test entropy over training batches, not test error over epochs.
Not tested. Students get more data, but the labels also change, and there is no controlled sample-size sweep.
Only random ReLU features on binary MNIST (and simulated Gaussian data). No other non-neural model classes.
Variance as a separate driver, multiple or triple descent, and removal of the peak by optimally tuned regularization are not tested. Only 0/10/20% noise on CIFAR-10.

missing.what: Random ReLU teacher on simulated 50-dimensional Gaussian data (250 examples): classification error versus number of features, with the text saying double descent 'kicks in'.
Stated memorization (interpolation) points: about m=10 for CIFAR-10 and SVHN, and m=20 for both ImageNet runs. Needed to compare peak location with the interpolation threshold.
Bias-variance optimum of the ImageNet ResNet50 teacher at about m=5, and the teacher curve repeated with students from m=5, 15 and 64 teachers.
Five-run mean and range for CIFAR-10 student test-error curves, showing the single run is representative.

record.verdict_notes: The paper uses double descent as a premise, but its teacher sweeps are standard width-wise tests. All curves are figure-only single runs (Adam, constant LR 1e-4, no early stopping). The CIFAR-10 absence at 0% noise matches Nakkiran's observation that the peak is weak without label noise. Read V1 'challenges' together with the V6 noise result. Student rows confound sample size with teacher-label quality.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests model-wise curves in its specified settings, not all deep-network architectures or settings.
Test error over training epochs; Figure 6 reports entropy over training batches instead.
No controlled sweep of training sample size measuring test error near the interpolation threshold.
The study tests random ReLU feature models and deep CNN/ResNet settings, not a broad range of non-neural model classes or whether the classical U-shaped curve is subsumed generally.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

The study varies injected label noise on CIFAR-10 and reports a shift in the hump. It does not test multiple or triple descent, variance as a separate cause, or optimally tuned regularization eliminating the peak.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters.
